headline: Two-person startup fixes one of modern life's most hated sounds: the microwave beep
summary: Sound designers Joel Corelitz and Colin Coogan from Starling have developed a code-only solution to replace the shrill microwave beep with pleasant, varied tones, using existing hardware.
details: Many people dread the shrill beep of a microwave oven, often rushing to open the door before it sounds. Sound designers Joel Corelitz and Colin Coogan of Starling aimed to eliminate this universally disliked noise. They found a way to improve the kitchen experience sonically without any hardware changes.

Corelitz and Coogan, known for their work with Sony, Microsoft, and Ford, tackled the microwave beep problem. Their solution manipulates existing microcontrollers and passive piezoelectric buzzers through software, proving that better sounds are possible with current technology.

For decades, nearly all microwaves have used cheap passive piezoelectric buzzers, first popularized by Japanese manufacturers in the 1970s. These simple devices vibrate a membrane to produce a basic beep, costing only cents and widely used in many gadgets.

Despite their limitations, manufacturers continue to use these buzzers due to fierce competition and cost-saving measures in consumer white goods. Adding more sophisticated speakers would increase costs, a barrier for many appliance makers.

Starling's challenge was to create better, more personalized microwave sounds using only code, without adding new hardware. Corelitz states that any microcontroller accepting C++ can be reprogrammed to produce different sounds, leveraging the existing microcontroller and piezo buzzer.

Using their "Microwave Sound Bench" software, Corelitz demonstrated alternatives like short trills, frequency sweeps, and arpeggios. These new sounds, which resemble video game effects, are a significant improvement over the traditional cortisol-inducing beeps.

The solution is theoretically compatible with any existing microwave hardware, requiring only manufacturers to update the device's code. Their test setup uses an Arduino UNO R4 Minima microcontroller and a breadboard with three piezo buzzers.

headline_marked: [[Leaked Radeon RX 9050]] hints at 4GB VRAM return in 2026, also 8GB config spotted
headline: Leaked Radeon RX 9050 hints at 4GB VRAM return in 2026, also 8GB config spotted
summary: ASRock listings reveal AMD's rumored RX 9050 GPU in 4GB and 8GB configurations, potentially bringing back 4GB VRAM cards not seen since 2022.
details: ASRock has reportedly listed the rumored Radeon RX 9050 on its website in two different configurations: 4GB and 8GB. While AMD has made no official announcements, these leaked specs suggest the return of 4GB VRAM GPUs in 2026, a memory pool not seen in new cards since 2022.
The RX 9050 appears to utilize a cut-down Navi 44 GPU, featuring 1,024 cores spread across 16 Compute Units. ASRock's Challenger variant lists a 1,920 MHz base clock and a 2,600 MHz boost clock.

The 4GB variant's listing notes 4GB of GDDR6 VRAM operating over a 64-bit bus, providing a bandwidth of 144 GB/s. This contrasts with current-gen cards, which have largely adopted 8GB as a baseline, a capacity already criticized for its future-proofing.

The 8GB variant's specifications indicate double the bandwidth at 288 GB/s, thanks to its 128-bit-wide bus. It is possible AMD plans to sell the 8GB model directly to consumers while limiting the 4GB variant to OEMs.

The leaked images show a generic design with a black shroud, silver accents, and RGB lighting. The card includes two DisplayPort 2.1a and one HDMI 2.1b ports, powered by a single 8-pin PCIe connector. The 8GB model is expected to handle 1080p gaming effectively, benefiting from RDNA 4 architecture features like improved ray tracing and FSR 4.
